clinicalPearls: Presents as a progressive or relapsing symmetric polyneuropathy evolving over at least 8 weeks, distinguishing it from Guillain-Barre syndrome which peaks by 4 weeks
Weakness typically affects both proximal and distal muscles, unlike the length-dependent pattern of most axonal neuropathies
Large-fiber sensory loss (vibration, proprioception) predominates over pain, and reflexes are diffusely diminished or absent
Cranial nerve and autonomic involvement can occur but are less prominent and severe than in Guillain-Barre syndrome
CSF classically shows albuminocytologic dissociation (elevated protein with normal cell count), similar to acute demyelinating polyneuropathy
Electrodiagnostic studies showing multifocal demyelination (conduction block, temporal dispersion, prolonged distal latencies, slowed conduction velocities) are central to diagnosis
A meaningful subset responds to immunotherapy, so early recognition matters because untreated disease can lead to irreversible axonal loss and disability
Some patients have an underlying paraprotein, diabetes, HIV, or other systemic association that should be screened for
harrison.pathophysiology: CIDP results from a T-cell and antibody-mediated autoimmune attack on peripheral nerve myelin and, in some cases, the nodal/paranodal region, producing segmental demyelination and secondary remyelination with onion-bulb formation. Some patients harbor antibodies against paranodal proteins (e.g., neurofascin, contactin-1), which behave more like a nodopathy than classic demyelination and may predict differential treatment response. Chronic or repeated inflammatory injury can eventually cause secondary axonal degeneration, which correlates with residual disability.
additionalDifferentials: POEMS syndrome and other paraproteinemic neuropathies
Hereditary demyelinating neuropathies (e.g., Charcot-Marie-Tooth disease type 1)
Multifocal motor neuropathy with conduction block
Neuropathy associated with lymphoma, amyloidosis, or vasculitis
additionalInvestigations: Nerve conduction studies/EMG — demonstrates demyelinating features such as conduction block and slowed velocities
Lumbar puncture with CSF protein and cell count — supports diagnosis via albuminocytologic dissociation and helps exclude infection or malignancy
Serum protein electrophoresis with immunofixation — screens for an associated monoclonal gammopathy
Fasting glucose/HbA1c — evaluates for coexisting diabetic neuropathy that can confound the picture
Nerve biopsy (selected cases) — shows demyelination and onion-bulb formation when diagnosis remains uncertain
Anti-paranodal antibody testing (e.g., neurofascin-155, contactin-1) — identifies a nodopathy subgroup with distinct treatment response
MRI of spinal nerve roots/plexus with contrast — may show root or plexus enhancement/hypertrophy supporting a proximal demyelinating process
HIV and hepatitis serologies — excludes infectious associations
redFlags: Rapidly progressive weakness with respiratory compromise mimicking Guillain-Barre syndrome requires urgent evaluation and monitoring
Significant axonal loss on electrodiagnostic testing suggests a worse prognosis and need for prompt treatment escalation
Asymmetric or purely motor presentations should prompt consideration of multifocal motor neuropathy rather than CIDP
Coexisting monoclonal gammopathy warrants hematologic workup to exclude POEMS syndrome or malignancy
Lack of any response to appropriate first-line immunotherapy should trigger diagnostic reconsideration
pitfalls: Mistaking CIDP for a slowly evolving Guillain-Barre syndrome, or vice versa, based solely on time course without full electrodiagnostic correlation
Over-reliance on CSF protein elevation alone, which is nonspecific and can be seen in diabetes and other conditions
Missing an underlying paraproteinemia or nodopathy antibody profile that changes expected treatment response
Attributing residual deficits solely to inadequate treatment when secondary axonal degeneration has already occurred
harrison.prognosis: Most patients improve substantially with timely immunotherapy, though relapses are common and some require long-term maintenance treatment. Delayed diagnosis or predominant axonal involvement is associated with greater residual disability.
references: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine, 22e — Chapter on Guillain-Barre Syndrome and Other Immune-Mediated Neuropathies
management: Induce remission with first-line immunotherapy — corticosteroids, intravenous immunoglobulin, or plasma exchange — chosen by severity and comorbidity
Maintain response with periodic intravenous or subcutaneous immunoglobulin, tapering to the lowest effective interval
Add steroid-sparing immunosuppression such as azathioprine, mycophenolate mofetil, or ciclosporin to limit long-term corticosteroid exposure
In anti-paranodal (neurofascin-155 or contactin-1) nodopathy, which responds poorly to immunoglobulin, consider rituximab
Provide physiotherapy, occupational therapy, gait aids, and neuropathic pain agents such as gabapentinoids or tricyclics for symptomatic support
Monitor with serial strength testing, disability scales, and nerve conduction studies to detect relapse and secondary axonal degeneration
Refer to a neuromuscular specialist and escalate or switch immunotherapy for refractory or worsening disease
